contentBody: **A report claims a machine's failure rate "tripled" based on failures going from 2 to 6 out of 50,000 units. What is the biggest risk in repeating this claim as-is?**
option.1: There is no risk; the arithmetic is correct so the claim is safe to repeat
option.2: The tiny sample size (2 to 6) makes "tripled" sound far more dramatic than it really is
option.3: Failure rates can never be expressed as percentages
option.4: The AI must have refused to answer this question
answerExplanation: The maths is technically right, but with such tiny counts the word "tripled" creates a false sense of alarm — checking the sample size behind a dramatic-sounding claim is a core sanity check.

contentBody: **Two events happened together: a website redesign launched, and sign-ups rose the same week. Which is the more careful way to describe this in a report?**
option.1: "Sign-ups rose the same week as the redesign; other causes have not yet been ruled out."
option.2: "The redesign caused the rise in sign-ups."
answerExplanation: Two things happening at the same time is correlation, not proof of causation — a careful report says what happened together and flags that the cause has not been confirmed.
